text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown has the rare luxury of not having to worry too much about the requirements for a single European currency, as he prepares for his first budget.

That is not because of Britain's stand offish attitude towards the grand plan, but because its fiscal position has improved so much the country would make the grade comfortably if it did want to join, analysts said.

"A lot of the European countries would love to have the fiscal position that Brown has," said Mark Wall, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "There's just not a match betwen the political will and the economics."
In many European countries, finance ministers are trying furiously to find ways to shrink budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product this year.
The Maastricht Treaty calls for a three percent deifict-to-GDP ratio and a 60 percent total debt-to-GDP share.

But the deficit rule has been vexing European authorities more than the total debt category, mainly because it is widely accepted that it will require more time to reduce the amount of debt in some countries.
"I don't think Brown is unduly concerned or will set his budget with one eye, or even half an eye, on what the Maastricht criteria require," said Andy Cates, UK economist at UBS in London.
Wall also said EMU would probably not feature much as a budget consideration. "I don't think there's going to be any explicit drive or any underlying theme in the budget to rush into EMU in 1999."
Under the Maastricht Treaty, the euro single currency is due to be launched in 1999. Economic performances in 1997 will be used to determine which countries are included in the first wave.

Economists said Britain's 1997-98 public sector borrowing requirement is likely to be smaller than the latest official forecast for 19.2 billion stg. The government also predicted a 2.5 percent deficit ratio.
On the total debt-to-GDP requirement, Britain is also set to come in under the 60 percent threshold.

Cates said UBS expects 18 billion stg for the PSBR, which technically is slightly different from the budget deficit. Britain's deficit-to-GDP ratio is likely to be around three percent for this year, he said.
Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley in London, forecast a 15 billion stg PSBR in the current year ending March 31, 1998 and a nine billion stg PSBR the year after that.
"Both in 1997 and 1998 that would imply meeting the three pct criterion," Miller said.
But economists said expectations Britain would qualify for EMU, even though it is highly unlikely to join in the first wave, have little to do with considerations that go beyond domestic shores.

"The need to balance the public finances as laid down in a medium term (domestic) strategy will be first and foremost," Miller said. He said that as a "by-product" that would leave Brown in a good position regarding Maastricht.
